newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD-UK stocks mired in rate uneasiness.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD-UK stocks mired in rate uneasiness.

text.p: London shares face another week of thin trading next week as uncertainties about the interest rate outlook on both sides of the Atlantic and the British election keep investors sidelined, analysts said.

With Wall Street continuing its recent shaky trend and British rates widely expected to be raised shortly after the May 1 poll, shares are likely to struggle to make further progress in the short term, they said.

Stronger-than-expected U.S. inflation figures on Friday acted as a reminder that U.S. rates, jacked up by a quarter-point on March 25, could also be raised by a further quarter point at the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting on May 20.
"It could be a bad week, led by trends in the U.S.," said Nick Glydon, chart analyst at investment bank Robert Fleming.

Glydon pointed out that any sharp falls on Wall Street were still likely to drag European markets lower despite Europe's better rate prospects. "The longer term outlook in the U.S. is deteriorating," he said.

Yet with the FTSE 100 having made steady progress for much of the past week and British shares seen as more cheaply valued than major continental European markets, a significant sell-off is also regarded as unlikely.
"We have been recommending an overweight position on the UK, said Ian Scott, stock market strategist at U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers.
"We don't think the UK equity market is particularly cheap -- but in contrast, markets in continental Europe look expensive."
After dropping to a two-month low of 4,200.5 on April 1, the FTSE 100 nudged higher for much of the past two weeks to reach a peak of 4,335.1 on April 11 -- its highest level since the end of March.

Yet trading volumes remained depressed for much of that period and dealers were reluctant to read any fundamental change of sentiment into the advance, though the cash holdings of institutional funds remain high -- cash that could be injected into the market on any dips.

A hefty batch of UK economic pointers next week including unemployment and inflation reports for March is not expected to make a significant difference to prospects for a post-election rate rise and is not seen having a major impact on UK equities.
"It seems clear that rates need to go up after the election and I don't see the data having major effect when there is so much else going on," said Scott at Lehman.

Wednesday's unemployment figures are expected to show a decline of 45,000 following a 68,000 fall the previous month, while Thursday's retail price report is expected to show a 0.4 percent monthly rise leaving the annual inflation rate at 2.7 percent.
The underlying annual inflation rate, excluding mortgage interest payments, is seen edging lower to 2.8 percent from 2.9 percent the month before.
Also next week Monday's producer price report is expected to show output prices up 1.2 percent on the year before.
In the U.S. a batch of economic reports includes consumer prices for March along with industrial production and capacity utilisation.
Only one FTSE 100 company reports during the week -- automotive group LucasVarity Plc
